question: In July 2025, the Italian Government approved, with parliamentary majority support, to postpone to 2038 the decommissioning of Brindisi’s ‘Federico II’ coal-fired thermal power station, which is located in one of southern Italy’s most environmentally vulnerable industrial areas.

This decision goes against the climate neutrality objectives enshrined in the European Green Deal and puts at risk local decarbonisation pathways that are already under way through reindustrialisation plans, investments in renewables and projects supported by EU funds.
The power station, which is among those with the highest CO₂ emissions in Europe, contributes significantly to air pollution and worsening health conditions for residents. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider postponing the closure of the Brindisi plant to 2038 to be compatible with the objectives and obligations of the European Green Deal and the Fit for 55 % package?
Will it assess whether Italy has breached its commitments on the energy transition and decarbonisation, including in relation to the EU funding received?
What measures will it put in place to ensure that areas that are critical in terms of industry and the environment, such as Brindisi, are not excluded from the trajectory towards climate neutrality?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.10.2025) It is not possible at this stage to appraise the consequences of the mentioned extension in time as the actual eventual use for energy production capacity reserve is not stated.

In relation to emissions of pollutants from the Brindisi plant, they are regulated by the Industrial Emissions Directive1, as well as by the applicable Best Available Techniques Conclusions2. This said, the Commission monitors the progress of all Member States, including Italy, towards the 2030 target, including through the annually revised Climate Action Progress Report.

In the case of Italy, the Commission has issued specific observations in its National Energy and Climate Plan (PNIEC) in order to accelerate the energy transition of the Member State, and has called for a faster roll-out of renewable energy sources in Italy’s 2025 Country Specific Recommendations.

Power plants - such as the one mentioned - fall under the EU Emission Trading System (ETS); the total amount of ETS emission allowances decreases annually by 4.3% until 2027, thus ensuring the decarbonisation of the sectors subject to ETS as a whole. The EU ETS cap is set to bring emissions down by 62% by 2030 compared to 2005 levels emissions.

The Commission closely monitors the implementation of the Ambient Air Quality Directives3. On 10 November 2020, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled4 that Italy has breached the Directive because of systematic exceedances of the limit values for PM10 and because it did not adopt appropriate measures to keep the exceedance period as short as possible.
The Brindisi plant is part of air quality zone IT1613 Area Industriale and part of this infringement case.
